articles.title: ‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true?
articles.summary: A spate of serious safety incidents have increased fears about the power and impenetrability of the most advanced models. Picture humanity in a boat being swept down a raging river, praying there is no Niagara Falls ahead.
body: These were two of the analogies used this week by Prof Robert Trager, an expert in the nascent field of AI governance, to describe the perilous but potential-filled moment the world stands at with accelerating artificial intelligence.

Trager, the director of the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, was speaking in the week OpenAI claimed the technology had crossed the threshold known as AGI – artificial general intelligence – with its newest model, GPT-6 Astra.

That claim came as the company prepared for a potential $850bn (£630bn) stock flotation, so included a dose of marketing spin, but if true it may be significant. The San Francisco company defines AGI as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.

The tasks it claims Astra can automate include designing circuit boards, filling out tax returns, building video games, financial modelling, engineering design and helping assemble legal documents. The threat to some white-collar jobs is implicit.

articles.title: A city break in Łódź, Poland’s capital of cinema and factories
articles.summary: The imposing red-brick mills of its industrial past are a stunning example of urban regeneration in the former ‘city of a thousand chimneys’ Sometimes travel delivers a real shock.
body: Sometimes travel delivers a real shock. I’m moving along the boulevards in the Polish city of Łódź, enjoying the excellent cafes and warm sunshine, when I spot the vans. They are parked up on the verge, with racks of clothing and heavily laden tables behind. I can’t resist a Sunday morning market and walk towards a group of men huddled around a car that is covered in blankets. And then it happens. They turn – and I see they are weighing pistols in their hands. I recognise the lean profile of a German Luger, and then the bulkier Colt 45.

There is a second of doubt. I hesitate. They replace the weapons on the display and walk away laughing. I approach. On the car roof is a row of dusty soldiers’ helmets. “We were repairing a pavement in the centre of town,” says the seller cheerfully, handing me a badge to inspect. “Imagine! For 80 years, all this stuff was just under our feet.”

It’s a Wehrmacht shoulder badge from Kuban 1943, a last-ditch post-Stalingrad action on the Crimean peninsula. Who wore this, I wonder? A veteran of the Russian front who almost made it home? Nothing is clear, except that in Łódź, the past is never far away.
points: The imposing red-brick mills of its industrial past are a stunning example of urban regeneration in the former ‘city of a thousand chimneys’ Sometimes travel delivers a real shock.

articles.title: Tim Dowling: my twice-daily baths are giving me a sinking feeling
articles.summary: It’s raining in our hallway. Could my louche bathing regime be behind the showers? August is the traditional time for something major to go wrong with my house. So I’m not surprised, as I’m getting dressed one morning, to hear the middle one shouting something about it raining in the hallway.
body: “What?” I say, standing on the landing with a shirt half pulled over my head. “What do you mean?”
I look down to see that water is indeed falling from the ceiling in a rain-like fashion, leaving a giant puddle on the floorboards near the front door. “That ain’t good,” I say.

I go upstairs to the bathroom where, some minutes earlier, I had been reading in the bath. Beneath the big claw-foot tub is another puddle: evidently my bathwater emptied straight on to the floor, and then straight through the floor.
“Since when is that happening?” my wife says, coming out with a mop.
points: Could my louche bathing regime be behind the showers?

articles.title: The unsettling rise of cat seducers: ‘My little companion was missing – and I was consumed with anger’
articles.summary: Has your cat been gaining weight and staying out at night, only to arrive home reeking of marijuana? These are just some of the signs that a neighbour is trying to entice them away... When Amy’s cat, Sid*, first started spending more time away from home, Amy* put it down to wanderlust.
body: Sid is roaming – but most of the time, for entire afternoons and even sometimes overnight, he is with Amy’s neighbour. “He is in her house, constantly, all the time,” she says. This is not a coincidence. Sid might not be getting six dinners, like his famous namesake in Inga Moore ’s 1990 children’s book, but the neighbour is certainly spoiling him, as she recently let slip to Amy’s partner. “She’s feeding him organic chicken!” Amy says indignantly.

Amy does not blame Sid for being disloyal. “Cats are cats – they have no concept of human boundaries.” But her neighbour, she says, is overstepping by rewarding Sid’s visits despite frequent – and increasingly firm – requests to stop. “She’s literally enticing him away.”

articles.title: Pumpkin Chili
articles.summary: A can of pumpkin puree adds richness, body, and an autumnal hue to this speedy chili, letting the flavors of the spices, aromatics, and ground beef shine.
body: This pumpkin chili gets an entire can of pumpkin purée—but you’d hardly know it. Rather than making the chili taste like pumpkin, the purée gives it velvety richness, body, and an autumnal hue. (Be sure to buy pure pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling.) Best of all, it comes together on the stovetop in just 35 minutes, making it an easy weeknight dinner that’s equally at home on game day or Halloween.

One unusual step makes this quick chili work: Instead of browning the ground beef separately, you’ll cook it directly in the spiced pumpkin mixture. This keeps the meat tender during the short cook time while a vigorous stir breaks it down into chunky, satisfying bits. Worcestershire sauce brings in plenty of savory depth. Top each bowl with sour cream, sliced jalapeño, and crunchy toasted pepitas.
Yes. Ground turkey and chicken both work well, but ground pork makes an especially rich, savory chili. Swap an equal amount of any of these for the beef and otherwise follow the recipe as written.
Yes. Canned butternut squash or even sweet potato works well here—just make sure it’s 100% purée, not pie mix or otherwise sweetened.

articles.title: The Last-Chance Tourism of Iceland's Glacier Raves
articles.summary: From eclipse-viewing festivals to exclusive raves set inside a glacier, the chance to party amid natural phenomena is a new type of luxury.
body: Weaving through the crowd, I pause next to Kali Van Horn, a 30-year-old architect from Brooklyn with glitter dripping from her eyes like crystallized tears. We share the moment as strangers, pressing our backs against the frozen wall as two DJs spin house and techno tracks in the heart of Langjökull—Iceland’s second-largest glacier.

“It’s healing,” Van Horn says, as rainbow lights illuminate the ice cave’s blue hues. Surrounding us are people wearing winter coats accessorized with light-up scarves, sparkly snowflake-shaped sunglasses, and hoods lined with lavender fur.
A performer sings at the Iceland Eclipse festival in remote Hellissandur, on Snæfellsnes Peninsula.
Many of the more than 3,000 attendees travel great distances to get to western Iceland.

articles.title: Angie Nixon Has Big Senate Dreams—But Her Feet Are Firmly on the Ground (in Hot Pink Skechers)
articles.summary: The Democratic candidate for the Florida Senate talks campaign-trail style, scoring an AOC endorsement, rising above racist criticism and more.
body: If you want to find time with Angie Nixon, you might just have to do it while she’s driving. The 42-year-old labor organizer and member of the Florida House of Representatives won the Democratic Party’s Senate nomination last month, and between hitting the campaign trail and raising five children, Nixon—only the second Black woman to win a major party nomination for the US Senate in Florida—is often on the road.

That’s exactly where Vogue caught up with her this week to learn about the lessons she’s learned as a small business owner that she hopes to take with her to the Senate, the progressive politicians she’s modeling herself after, her focus on youth mental health, and the campaign-trail insult that she and her team turned into a signature look.
Vogue: What has life looked like since your Senate primary win last month?
I saw you recently got Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s endorsement. What has it been like to build that relationship?

articles.title: I'm Obsessed With the 'Conversate' App on These Smart Glasses
articles.summary: I am obsessed with the "Conversate" app in my Even Realities G2 smart glasses. Overall, the glasses are sci-fi cool —they project a small, monochrome HUD in front of your eyes but look like normal glasses—but Conversate is essential.
body: We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

If you've ever left a work meeting thinking, "wait, am I supposed to file the TPS reports, or is it Gary's week?" consider Conversate. I don't multi-task well, so listening while taking notes can be difficult. Conversate solves that problem.

When the meeting is over, you can check out a summary of what was discussed, and Conversate will highlight anything that looks like a task for you. You can then take those tasks and migrate them to your glasses' to-do list with a click, so you have a checkable list of action items floating before your eyes whenever you want it.
I realize that all of these functions could be done with a number of smart phone apps, but with Conversate, you keep your phone in your pocket—much more unobtrusive.

articles.title: Steal My Food Itinerary: A Long Weekend in Upstate New York
articles.summary: I love New York City in the summer, especially this past one, but I grew up in the shadow of the Rocky Mountains. I’m in my late 20s, I rock climb, and I live in Brooklyn, so of course I have an upstate New York itinerary for you. My partner’s mom’s partner (yes) has a
body: Heading upstate this fall for autumn hikes and apple picking? Don’t sleep on all of the farm-to-table restaurants that the region has to offer.

When I tell people in the city about my trips upstate, they’re often surprised to hear me gush about the restaurants. And while I think you could make all your meals (the bounty at the farm stands and markets make cooking very dreamy up there) and still have a great time, I can also strongly make the case for a dining-focused trip. Here’s where to go.

If you’re heading up from the city, there are a few transit options (a bus from Port Authority to New Paltz or Kingston, the Metro North to Poughkeepsie, Amtrak to Hudson), but you’ll want a car to get around once you’re in the Catskills. I journey upstate via a car, which we pick up in New Jersey; that means that I get to grab Corner Slice’s massive, pillowy garlic knots as a pre-trip snack. If you find yourself in the area, I recommend you do the same.
